title: The real dichotomy in sandbox games isn't quests vs. no quests — it's whether the world is causally legible.
author: Patient_Street_8437
selftext:
I'm not a dev, just a player, but I recently realized that what makes some sandbox games feel directionless to me is not necessarily the lack of quests.

The real issue is that, as a new player, I often don't understand the causal structure of the world yet.

Take Project Zomboid as an example. I know the goal is to survive, but at the beginning I don't know what I should be preparing for. How safe is this house? How strong are the doors? What will become scarce? What systems will fail later? What should I do now to prevent a problem several days from now?

An experienced player already knows this, so when they look at a house they don't just see a house. They see entry points, escape routes, vulnerabilities, future storage, access to water, risks from noise, etc.

That's what I mean by a causally legible world.

I don't think the solution has to be more quests. The game could communicate this through lore, radio broadcasts, environmental storytelling, NPC dialogue, abandoned camps, failed defenses, corpses, notes, and visible consequences.

Instead of giving me a quest saying "Find a generator", let me hear that the electrical grid is becoming unstable. Let me find a note saying someone moved their food somewhere with a generator.

Now I understand:

power may fail → refrigeration matters → generators matter → fuel matters

And suddenly I create my own quests.

I think a good sandbox doesn't always need to tell the player what to do. It needs to teach the player what makes a difference in that world.

Once the causal structure becomes clear enough, the "quest" starts forming naturally in the player's mind.

comments.author: Patient_Street_8437
comments.body: Meaningful progression does not come from having more things to unlock. It comes from understanding what future problems those unlocks are meant to solve.

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
Project Zomboid may be an odd example to use since that game's entire premise is "learn by dying", just like its main inspiration (CDDA) and Soulsborne games. They purposely don't tell you things that they easily could. I call it "iterative gameplay": You throw yourself into it, fail, learn from the failure, and change how you play next time.

The big issue with making a good sandbox game is keeping the game fun and engaging even when people have hundreds/thousands of hours in it and know all the mechanics and "gotchas". That's one reason why the popular ones always have some type of procgen component (Zomboid, Minecraft, Terraria, CDDA, etc.). They're able to keep each time through it fresh because you can't just go to the same place every time and find a strong item.

replies.author: Warrmak
replies.body:
is it a big issue?   what percentage of player's are playing a game to the point where they master every mechanic to the point where they can survive in perpetuity? 

I'd venture to guess that the "hardcore" players are probably a small percentage of all players, but a large percentage of persistent players.

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body:
Even if the difficulty ramps up, if the sequence becomes boring and known, then there feels like little point to playing again and again. Procgen worlds make it different each time.

Deckbuilding games like StS rely on different pathing and a large card pool and card synergy mechanics; Balatro does it by joker and effect variety and synergy. Static RPGs do maybe by different choices and endings - think Chrono trigger. But no one wants to sit there “mastering” a skill in a game unless there is a new or different reward or experience each time

replies.author: Warrmak
replies.body: Mastering skills from a stick skills perspective, or skill tree perspective?

replies.author: darkoblivion000
replies.body: From your comment I was inferring you meant players mastering skills needed to be proficient in the game

replies.author: Warrmak
replies.body: Ehhhh not necessarily one or the other.   I think learning the hidden mechanics and systems and lore are all all part of player retention. But I understand that any one of those things alone might not be enough.

comments.author: ZeColorOfPomegranate
comments.body: As for me, I would LOVE to play a Far Cry 2-grade game - dark, mature, pessimistic. That's probably because I'm 42...
